Senses.Explanation: The three-inch tongue is the speaking organ, often shortened in Chan exchanges to just 'the three inches.' Baoning Renyong supplies the full form: 'I have one mouth, containing a three-inch tongue; the teeth are all complete, and there is no right and wrong it does not speak' (我有一張口，內含三寸舌。牙齒總完全，是非無不說). An unnamed questioner asks Cuiyan Lingcan to speak 'without borrowing the three inches' (不借三寸，請師道), and another unnamed questioner calls Dahui Zonggao's 'three inches' tightly guarded (老和尚三寸甚密). The omitted noun is recoverable from the explicit full form and from the predicates of speaking. The Zen bend is this use of an ordinary measure as public shorthand for the tongue, not a claim that every occurrence of three inches names speech.
Senses.Note: This sense is not split into praise and criticism of speech; those are different readings of the same tongue referent.

AlternateTargets: three inches in distance or thickness
Senses.Explanation: Three inches is a measure whose object and dimension are supplied by its construction. In the Boatman's case, Chuanzi Decheng says, 'the line hangs a thousand feet, its intent in the deep pool; three inches from the hook, why do you not speak?' (垂絲千尺，意在深潭，離鉤三寸，子何不道). Zhang Shangying's verse preserves the same distance from the hook. Fozhao Deguang uses the measure for thickness when he says Huangbo's facial skin remains three inches thick (面皮厚三寸). Tianru Weize's mortality warning applies the same small-span image to breath: 'when the three-inch breath is cut off, one fire burns through' (三寸氣斷，一火洞然). Distance, thickness, and the measured-breath image differ in what is measured, not in the lexical value of three inches; they therefore remain one sense rather than three context-driven senses.
Senses.Note: The fishing construction is not reassigned to the tongue merely because speech follows it. Conversely, face-skin and breath supply their own measured nouns and do not create new bare-headword meanings. The separately retained tongue sense is supported by genuine noun omission in bare public-interview uses.

Occurrences.Kwic: 垂絲千尺。意在深潭。離鉤三寸。子何不道。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Compendium of the Five Lamps (五燈會元), Chuanzi Decheng section. Chuanzi Decheng is the exact speaker who says the line hangs a thousand feet and asks why the student does not speak when three inches from the hook.

Occurrences.Kwic: 蘆葦蕭蕭江岸秋，長天獨月向西流。離鈎三寸無人道，笑倚蘭橈自點頭。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Classified Collection of the Chan Grove (禪林類聚) explicitly marks this verse 'Layman Wujin said' (無盡居士云). Zhang Shangying, Layman Wujin, is the exact verse author: his boat verse says that three inches from the hook no one speaks, while the boatman smiles and nods against the oar.
